Today, we have a few key objectives. The first is to talk about pre-processing your data. This is super important. Some of you asked me how you actually process your data. Before we even talk about different algorithms, a very important machine learning workflow is to understand how to convert or process your data. There are two types of data: numerical data and categorical data.

You will see on Saturday, in a practical sense, when I give you the Kaggle competition to predict HDB prices, you will see that you have over 70 datasets. Some datasets are numerical, like the size of your house, how high, what is the square feet of the house, the number of lease remaining years. Those are your numerical data. But most of the time, you also have categorical variables, like what kind of house it is: a 4-room flat, a 5-room resale flat, a mansionette.

A very important part of working with machine learning algorithms is to know how to handle the processing of this data, because different algorithms have different constraints. Some allow you to handle numerical data easily, some have challenges with certain categorical variables. The whole idea here is to familiarize yourself with the different mechanisms to process this data. We're only going to introduce some basic ones, but you can explore more advanced methods.

Keywords: data preprocessing, numerical data, categorical data, HDB prices, feature engineering, machine learning workflow, data types

The second thing we need to discuss, which is also very important, is success metrics. From a data science standpoint, there are two types of metrics we are always very interested in. The first is, as a data scientist, what kind of metrics can you measure from the performance of your model? This is usually what we call the offline machine learning-based metrics. These metrics are important because they give you direction and tell you the progress of your models. You need to be able to measure if what you are doing—the data you have chosen, the processing you have done, the training of the model—actually works. You need some form of metric to reason about whether the model is trained correctly and if the prediction will work. That's usually what we call the offline machine learning metrics.

In reality, you have your offline metrics, which are the technical ones. But in reality, you also have an online metric. We are not talking about online metrics right now, but does anybody know an example of an online metric in business? If a company were to hire you to build a machine learning model, what kind of online metrics do you think the company would care about? Offline metrics are very technical. What about online metrics?

Keywords: machine learning metrics, success metrics, model performance, offline metrics, online metrics, data science metrics, model evaluation

If you're Mark Zuckerberg, you will care about things like your click-through rate. How many people are clicking? If I show the ads, are people clicking on the ads? These are online metrics that are business-related. We call them online metrics because we cannot measure them offline. Unless you have some kind of simulated environment, it's very unlikely that you can measure the online metric. The online metric, as the name suggests, needs to be derived from an experimentation. This ties back to 3.1: why must you do hypothesis testing? Why must you know about all the statistical tests? Because you're going to do some A-B testing. You're going to expose a portion of the model that you have built, and you are going to measure some of the business impact. This can only be measured online. Our focus is on the offline metric, which is, from a technical data science perspective, even before we know whether the algorithm works and provides business value, you need to know whether it works offline first. In your offline setting, does the model train? Is the model trained correctly? Is the model able to make an accurate prediction? We'll talk about the offline metrics. On Thursday, we will expand further about measurement. Today, we are just talking about what metrics are available, what are their trade-offs. On Thursday, we'll talk about how you actually perform the validation. All of this revolves around the offline setting, which means today, in your own workflow, you can actually make that kind of measurement. You can go to your team after the POC and say that, in terms of offline metrics, I have some performance. Sometimes, in reality, it can be a very good indicator of your model. Sometimes it's correlated to the online metric, sometimes, unfortunately, it's not. Sometimes they can be correlated, sometimes they might not, because ultimately, what you're measuring sometimes is not the business metric. The three paradigms you need to think about in terms of machine learning value are the offline, the online, and the engineering metrics. Engineering metrics, people talk about latency. If it's a real-time machine learning system, people will look at the P99, prediction latency, whether it's X number of milliseconds. Why is it important? If you think about your app, when you're using the app as a consumer, you expect it to be very responsive, very fast. If there are some decisions behind the app you're using, be it booking a car, booking a ride, ordering food, you wouldn't want to see the screen turning and spinning and telling you, "please wait." You want the experience to be very smooth. If behind the scenes there's a machine learning algorithm powering the experience, then the engineering metrics need to be considered. That's a takeaway for this slide.

Am I able to solve this problem using machine learning? After that, you will start to do your EDA to understand more about the data. Before you throw it into a machine learning algorithm, you need to start to do some processing. It should be intuitive that EDA and preprocessing are hand-in-hand. When you do EDA, how you should be preprocessing the data should be related. You shouldn't be knowing what to preprocess without doing the EDA, because you need to understand the kind of data you have, and if there are some issues with the data before you think about preprocessing it. Essentially, you can see this preprocessing flow.
